- I added up the estimates for all 18,638 census block groups in Texas.
- This is a survey estimate averaged over five years, so it has some sampling error. It's not the same as the official 2020 Census count.
- I took "Texas" to mean the state. If you meant Texas County, Missouri or Texas County, Oklahoma, let me know.

Source: ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020), B01003 (Total population), field B01003e1, summed over block groups.

I estimate the median household income in King County, WA at about **$99,300** (ACS 2020 5-year release, 2016–2020, in 2020 dollars). I calculated this myself, so it's not an official Census median.

**Why there's no exact county median**
- The median household income field (B19013e1) only gives one value per block group, which is a small neighborhood area. King County has **1,545 block groups**, and **1,486** of them report a median. Those medians range from **$12,222** to **$250,001**, the field's top value.
- Medians from separate areas can't be added or averaged into a correct county median, so the exact figure can't be worked out from this data.

**How I estimated it**
- I added up the number of households in each income range across all King County block groups. That came to **900,061 households**.
- The middle household falls in the **$75,000–$99,999** range, very close to the top. Assuming incomes are spread evenly within that range gives about $99,300.
- Because the result is so close to $100,000, the real median could easily be on either side of it.

**Average for comparison:** The **average** household income is about **$134,700**: total household income ($121.2 billion) divided by 900,061 households. It's well above the median because high incomes pull the average up. About 170,181 households (18.9%) earn $200,000 or more.

All of these are survey estimates, so they have sampling error.

Source: ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020), B19001 (Household Income, fields B19001e1–B19001e17), B19025 (Aggregate Household Income, field B19025e1) and B19013 (Median Household Income, field B19013e1, checked to confirm it's only reported by block group), King County block groups (GEOID prefix 53033); median estimated from the income ranges as described above.

I can't show change since 2010 because this dataset has no 2010 figures. It holds only two ACS 5-year releases: 2019 (covering 2015–2019) and 2020 (covering 2016–2020). The closest comparison I can make is between those two:

| Release | Survey years | California population |
|---|---|---|
| ACS 2019 5-year | 2015–2019 | 39,283,497 |
| ACS 2020 5-year | 2016–2020 | 39,346,023 |
| **Difference** | | **+62,526 (+0.2%)** |

**Why this isn't a real one-year change:** The two releases share four of their five survey years (2016–2019). So the 62,526 difference mostly reflects swapping 2015 out for 2020, not growth from one year to the next. Each figure is also an estimate with sampling error. The Census Bureau advises comparing 5-year periods that don't overlap, and this dataset doesn't have any.

For a 2010-to-present trend, you'd need the 2010 and 2020 Decennial Census counts or the Census Bureau's annual population estimates. Neither is in this dataset.

Source: ACS 2019 5-year (2015–2019) and ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020), B01003 (Total population), field B01003e1, added up across California's block groups.

Florida's population estimate went up by **315,288 people (+1.5%)** from the 2019 release to the 2020 release.

| ACS 5-year release | Survey years | Florida population |
|---|---|---|
| 2019 | 2015–2019 | 20,901,636 |
| 2020 | 2016–2020 | 21,216,924 |
| **Change** | | **+315,288 (+1.5%)** |

**This isn't a one-year change.** Each release is a 5-year estimate, and these two share four of their five survey years (2016–2019). The only difference is that the 2020 release drops 2015 and adds 2020. So the 315,288 figure shows how the 5-year average moved, not how much Florida grew from 2019 to 2020. The Census Bureau recommends comparing 5-year periods that don't overlap. Since this dataset only has these two releases, that kind of comparison isn't possible here.

Source: ACS 2019 5-year (2015–2019) and ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020), B01003 (Total population), field B01003e1, summed over Florida block groups (state FIPS 12).

Cook County, IL had 20.3% of households with income under $25,000 in the 2019 release and 19.2% in the 2020 release. That is about 1.1 percentage points lower, or roughly 18,600 fewer households.

| Release | Survey years | Households | Under $25,000 | Share |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ACS 2019 5-year | 2015–2019 | 1,972,108 | 401,095 | 20.3% |
| ACS 2020 5-year | 2016–2020 | 1,991,474 | 382,543 | 19.2% |

**Why this isn't a simple one-year change:**
- **The releases share four of their five years (2016–2019).** The difference mostly reflects swapping 2015 for 2020, so it's not a year-over-year trend. The Census Bureau recommends comparing releases whose years don't overlap.
- **The dollar basis may differ.** The guidance for this dataset says each release reports income in its own year's dollars (2019 dollars vs. 2020 dollars), so the $25,000 cutoff isn't exactly the same in real terms. I couldn't confirm this from the data: the field labels say "2020 inflation-adjusted dollars" for both releases. I also can't measure how much inflation matters here, since there's no inflation data in this dataset.
- **There's sampling error.** These are survey estimates, so a gap of about one point should be read with some caution.

Source: ACS 2019 5-year (2015–2019) and ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020), B19001 (Household Income in the Past 12 Months). Fields B19001e1 (total) and B19001e2–e5 (under $25,000) were summed over Cook County block groups (GEOID prefix 17031).

_Note: an automated check couldn't confirm every figure above against the query results._

The 2020 release is 19,878 people (about 0.2%) higher. That difference is **not** a real year-over-year change, for two reasons:

Source: ACS 2019 5-year (2015–2019) and ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020), B01003 (Total population), field B01003e1, summed over block groups in Ohio (state FIPS 39).

The table below has the population and estimated median household income for all 50 states, DC and Puerto Rico. It uses the 2020 ACS 5-year release (2016–2020) and is sorted by population.

**About the income figures:** this dataset only has median income for each block group (small areas within a state). You can't get a state's exact median by combining those, so the state figures here are estimates. For each state, I added up its households in each of the 16 income ranges, found the range containing the middle household, and estimated the median within that range by straight-line interpolation. They're in 2020 dollars.

**Highlights:**
- **Most populous:** California (39,346,023), then Texas (28,635,442), Florida (21,216,924) and New York (19,514,849).
- **Least populous:** Wyoming (581,348), then Vermont (624,340) and DC (701,974).
- **Highest estimated median income:** DC (~$91,664), then Maryland (~$87,688), New Jersey (~$85,954) and Massachusetts (~$85,011).
- **Lowest estimated median income among the states:** Mississippi (~$46,573), then West Virginia (~$48,097) and Arkansas (~$49,498). Puerto Rico is much lower (~$21,095).

All figures are survey estimates and have sampling error.

Source: ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020). Population from B01003 (Total population), field B01003e1, summed over block groups. Median income estimated from B19001 (Household income), fields B19001e2–B19001e17, summed over block groups and interpolated within ranges. State names come from 2020_METADATA_CBG_FIPS_CODES.

The table below lists the population of all **3,221 counties and county-equivalents**, sorted from largest to smallest. The data comes from the ACS 2020 5-year release (2016–2020), the most recent one available. Together they add up to **329,824,950 people**.

- **What counts as a county:** The list includes the District of Columbia, independent cities such as Baltimore city and Virginia Beach city, Louisiana parishes, Alaska boroughs, and **78 Puerto Rico municipios** (3,255,642 people). Leave out Puerto Rico and there are 3,143 counties in the 50 states and DC, with a total of 326,569,308 people.
- **Largest:** Los Angeles County, CA is far ahead with 10,040,682 people. Next come Cook County, IL (5,169,517), Harris County, TX (4,680,609), Maricopa County, AZ (4,412,779) and San Diego County, CA (3,323,970).
- **Smallest:** Loving County, TX has just 117 people. King County, TX (279), Kenedy County, TX (391) and McPherson County, NE (420) are also very small.
- **Accuracy:** These are survey estimates averaged over 2016–2020. They are not the 2020 Census counts, so they carry sampling error. This matters most for very small counties.

Source: ACS 2020 5-year (2016–2020), B01003 (Total population), field B01003e1, summed over block groups by county code. County names are from "2020_METADATA_CBG_FIPS_CODES".
